items.followUp: Give four differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

rubric.why: Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus; eukaryotes have one.
rubric.description: Contrasts the nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct contrast.

rubric.why: Eukaryotic cells have membrane-bound organelles, unlike prokaryotic cells.
rubric.description: Contrasts membrane-bound organelles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct contrast.

rubric.why: Prokaryotic cells are generally smaller than eukaryotic cells.
rubric.description: Contrasts cell size.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct contrast.

rubric.why: Prokaryotic genetic material is typically circular, while eukaryotic nuclear chromosomes are linear.
rubric.description: Contrasts genetic material or chromosome organisation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct contrast.

modelAnswer: Prokaryotic cells have no true nucleus; their DNA lies in a nucleoid, whereas eukaryotic cells have a nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane.
Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles, whereas eukaryotic cells contain them, such as mitochondria.
Prokaryotic cells are generally smaller and simpler; eukaryotic cells are generally larger and more complex.
Prokaryotic DNA is usually circular and not organised into a membrane-bound nucleus; eukaryotic nuclear DNA is arranged in linear chromosomes.

items.followUp: Explain how an enzyme's active site determines which substrate it acts upon.

rubric.why: Specificity means an enzyme acts on a particular substrate or reaction.
rubric.description: Defines enzyme specificity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that an enzyme acts on a specific substrate or reaction.

rubric.why: The active site is the region responsible for substrate binding.
rubric.description: Identifies the active site as the binding region.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the active site.

rubric.why: The substrate fits the enzyme's active site because their shapes are complementary.
rubric.description: Explains the specific fit between substrate and active site.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the complementary fit or lock-and-key explanation.

rubric.why: Binding forms an enzyme-substrate complex.
rubric.description: States that enzyme and substrate form a complex.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the complex formation.

rubric.why: The reaction forms products, while the enzyme is not used up and can act again.
rubric.description: Describes the outcome and reuse of the enzyme.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for products being released and/or the enzyme remaining available for reuse.

modelAnswer: Enzyme specificity is the ability of an enzyme to act on a particular substrate or to catalyse a particular reaction.
Each enzyme has an active site with a particular shape.
Only a substrate with a complementary shape fits into that active site, like a key fitting a lock.
The substrate binds to the active site and forms an enzyme-substrate complex.
The reaction produces products, which are released; the enzyme remains unchanged and can be used again.

items.followUp: State how many ATP are formed in glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain during aerobic respiration of one glucose molecule.

rubric.why: Glycolysis yields a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose molecule.
rubric.description: Gives the ATP yield from glycolysis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 2 ATP from glycolysis.

rubric.why: The Krebs cycle yields 2 ATP per glucose molecule.
rubric.description: Gives the ATP yield from the Krebs cycle.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 2 ATP from the Krebs cycle.

rubric.why: The electron transport chain yields 34 ATP in the textbook energy budget.
rubric.description: Gives the ATP yield from the electron transport chain.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 34 ATP from the electron transport chain.

rubric.why: The textbook total is 38 ATP per glucose molecule.
rubric.description: Gives the total ATP yield.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct total.

modelAnswer: For the textbook energy budget of aerobic respiration, one glucose molecule yields:
Glycolysis: 2 ATP.
Krebs cycle: 2 ATP.
Electron transport chain: 34 ATP.
Total: 2 + 2 + 34 = 38 ATP per glucose molecule.

rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this function.

rubric.why: The liver helps remove or detoxify harmful substances from the blood.
rubric.description: States that the liver detoxifies harmful substances.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this function.

rubric.why: The liver deaminates excess amino acids and forms urea.
rubric.description: Describes deamination or urea formation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this function.

modelAnswer: The liver produces bile, which helps in the digestion of fats.
It stores glucose as glycogen and helps regulate the glucose level in the blood.
It detoxifies harmful substances in the blood.
It deaminates excess amino acids and converts the resulting nitrogenous waste into urea.
It stores vitamins and iron.

items.followUp: Explain the role of phloem in the movement of sugars from leaves to other parts of a plant.

rubric.why: Phloem is the tissue that transports food in plants.
rubric.description: Identifies phloem as the food-transport tissue.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming phloem or its sieve tubes.

rubric.why: Sugars made in leaves are transported as dissolved food, chiefly sucrose.
rubric.description: Identifies the transported food and its source.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that sugars/food made in leaves are transported.

rubric.why: Food moves from sources, such as leaves, to sinks such as growing or storage tissues.
rubric.description: Describes movement from source to sink.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct source-to-sink description.

rubric.why: This movement is translocation and involves loading and unloading sugars; active transport uses energy.
rubric.description: Names or explains the translocation process.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for translocation or a valid explanation of sugar loading/unloading.

modelAnswer: Food is transported through the phloem, mainly in its sieve tubes.
Sugars produced in the leaves during photosynthesis are loaded into the phloem, chiefly as sucrose.
The dissolved food moves from source regions, such as leaves, to sink regions, such as growing parts and storage organs; this movement is called translocation.
Sugars are unloaded at the sinks; loading and unloading may involve active transport and energy.

items.followUp: What makes a scientific theory useful and productive?

rubric.why: A theory is an explanation of natural phenomena supported by evidence.
rubric.description: Identifies a theory as an evidence-based explanation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing a theory as an explanation supported by evidence.

rubric.why: A productive theory generates testable predictions or new hypotheses.
rubric.description: Explains what makes the theory productive.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it produces testable predictions, new hypotheses, or further research.

modelAnswer: A scientific theory is an explanation of natural phenomena supported by evidence.
A productive theory leads to testable predictions or new hypotheses and helps guide further investigations.
